anatomy.intro: Long white hairs surround the ribbed green column and its stout colored spines.

parts.function: Long pale hairs form the conspicuous covering over the column.
parts.label: White hairs

parts.function: Orange to reddish-brown spines project beyond the hair covering.
parts.label: Stiff spine

parts.function: The ribbed stem beneath the hairs is the photosynthetic body.
parts.label: Green stem

parts.function: A new shoot at the base contributes to the species’ clumping habit.
parts.label: Basal side stem

flowers.text: Pink to red flowers around 4 cm long emerge near the upper part of mature stems, contrasting with the surrounding white hair.

growth.note: New shoots arise from the base, gradually turning a single hairy column into a clump.

stages.text: The young plant develops its white covering over a compact body.
stages.title: Small hairy stem

stages.text: The stem lengthens while colored spines remain visible through the hairs.
stages.title: Short column

stages.text: Side stems expand the group; mature growth can eventually produce flowers.
stages.title: Clumping plant

habitat.text: Native to dry mountainous regions of Bolivia and northwestern Argentina, this cactus grows a dense white coat around its green stems. Stiff orange to reddish-brown spines project through the hair.

image.alt: Old Man of the Andes cactus with numbered white hairs, projecting orange-brown spine, exposed green ribbed stem and basal side stem.

lookalikes.name: Feather cactus
lookalikes.text: Mammillaria plumosa makes a low mound covered by interlacing feather-like radial spines. Oreocereus instead has longer hair-like strands and obvious projecting orange-brown spines on columnar stems.

mature.text: The species forms a clump of short columns. Specialist descriptions give stems about 6–10 cm thick, usually under 50 cm high but occasionally approaching 1 m.

milestones.text: Joined the collection from Altman Reserve.
milestones.title: Acquired

nameStory.text: The accepted Oreocereus combination dates to 1936. Kew also records the original Cereus trollii name from 1929, showing how this Andean cactus has moved among genera in different treatments.
